contact_edits.before: This means that the dramatic climax has to be the story's start. The author lays out for herself the task of dramatizing the terrible day as it would have appeared to these people -- the casual turning on of the TV, the frantic telephoning that would be comic in another context, the overwhelming but temporary relief--and she brings it off with total conviction. A rather similar challenge confronts the actor who plays Jean, who only comes onstage halfway through, after what I can only describe as one hell of a retrospective buildup. This, too, is brilliantly met, with Jeff Irving conveying the essence of a walking nightmare, shifting between blankness and hysteria. There is a hint that one of the murdered women was his girlfriend, or at least that he would have liked her to be. (The hint is dropped twice: the only instance of the play's overplaying its hand.) The actual details of the massacre are sparingly mentioned, but they're omnipresent; we catch glimpses of them in Kathleen's bitter acknowledgment of how many lives were wrecked, even her irrational jealousy of how some other victims were buried. Christmas is a recurring image in the play. There could be many other ways of dramatizing that one horrific December day, but it's hard to believe that there could be one more effective. - In Toronto until May 17. For more information, call 416-368-3110.
